questions.q: A $30$ cm long solenoid has $10$ turns per cm and area of $5$ cm$^2$. The current through the solenoid coil varies from $2$ A to $4$ A in $3.14$ s. The e.m.f. induced in the coil is $\alpha\times 10^{-5}$ V. The value $\alpha$ is ________.
questions.solution:
Given:
Length of the solenoid, $l = 30 \text{ cm} = 0.3 \text{ m}$
Number of turns per unit length, $n = 10 \text{ turns/cm} = 1000 \text{ turns/m}$
Area of cross-section, $A = 5 \text{ cm}^2 = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$
Change in current, $\Delta I = 4 \text{ A} - 2 \text{ A} = 2 \text{ A}$
Time interval, $\Delta t = 3.14 \text{ s}$

The self-inductance of the solenoid is given by:
$L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$

Substituting the given values:
$L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (1000)^2 \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.3$
$L = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^6 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$
$L = 6\pi \times 10^{-5} \text{ H}$

The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is:
$e = L \dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$

Substituting the values of $L$, $\Delta I$, and $\Delta t$:
$e = 6\pi \times 10^{-5} \times \dfrac{2}{3.14}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:
$e = 6 \times 10^{-5} \times 2 = 12 \times 10^{-5} \text{ V}$

Comparing this with $e = \alpha \times 10^{-5} \text{ V}$, we get:
$\alpha = 12$

Answer: $12$

questions.q: A square loop of side $2$ cm is placed in a time varying magnetic field with magnitude as $B = 0.4\sin(300t)$ Tesla. The normal to the plane of loop makes an angle of $60°$ with the field. The maximum induced emf produced in the loop is __________ mV.
questions.solution:
Given:
Side of the square loop, $a = 2$ cm $= 2 \times 10^{-2}$ m
Area of the loop, $A = a^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^2$
Magnetic field, $B = 0.4 \sin(300t)$ T
Angle between the normal to the plane and the magnetic field, $\theta = 60^\circ$

The magnetic flux through the loop is given by:
$\Phi = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A} = B A \cos\theta$
$\Phi = (0.4 \sin(300t))(4 \times 10^{-4}) \cos(60^\circ)$
$\Phi = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} \sin(300t) \times \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\Phi = 0.8 \times 10^{-4} \sin(300t)$ Wb

By Faraday's law of induction, the induced emf is:
$e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$
$e = -\dfrac{d}{dt} (0.8 \times 10^{-4} \sin(300t))$
$e = -0.8 \times 10^{-4} \times 300 \cos(300t)$
$e = -240 \times 10^{-4} \cos(300t)$ V
$e = -24 \times 10^{-3} \cos(300t)$ V

The maximum induced emf is the amplitude of $e$:
$e_{\text{max}} = 24 \times 10^{-3}$ V $= 24$ mV

Answer: $24$

questions.q: An inductor of inductance $10$ mH having resistance of $100\,\Omega$ is connected to battery of E.M.F. $1.0$ V through a switch as shown in the figure below. After switch is closed, the ratio of instantaneous voltages across the inductor when the current passing through it is $2$ mA and $4$ mA is _______.
questions.solution:
In an LR circuit, the equation for the voltage is given by Kirchhoff's loop law:

$E = L \dfrac{di}{dt} + iR$

The instantaneous voltage across the ideal inductor is the induced EMF, which is given by:

$V_L = L \dfrac{di}{dt} = E - iR$

Given values are:
$E = 1.0$ V
$R = 100\,\Omega$

For current $i_1 = 2$ mA $= 2 \times 10^{-3}$ A, the voltage across the inductor is:

$V_{L1} = 1.0 - (2 \times 10^{-3} \times 100) = 1.0 - 0.2 = 0.8$ V

For current $i_2 = 4$ mA $= 4 \times 10^{-3}$ A, the voltage across the inductor is:

$V_{L2} = 1.0 - (4 \times 10^{-3} \times 100) = 1.0 - 0.4 = 0.6$ V

The ratio of the instantaneous voltages is:

$\dfrac{V_{L1}}{V_{L2}} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.6} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Answer: $4/3$

questions.q: A metal rod of length $L$ rotates about one end at origin with a uniform angular velocity $\omega$. The magnetic field radially falls off as $B(r) = B_0 e^{-\lambda r}$; $\lambda$ being a positive constant. The emf induced (neglecting the centripetal force on electrons in the rod) is :
questions.solution:
The motional emf $dE$ induced in a small element of length $dr$ at a distance $r$ from the origin is given by:

$dE = B(r) v(r) dr$

Since the rod is rotating with angular velocity $\omega$, the velocity of the element is $v(r) = \omega r$.

$dE = B_0 e^{-\lambda r} (\omega r) dr$

The total emf induced $E$ is the integral of $dE$ from $r = 0$ to $r = L$:

$E = \int_0^L B_0 \omega r e^{-\lambda r} dr$

$E = B_0 \omega \int_0^L r e^{-\lambda r} dr$

Using integration by parts:

$\int r e^{-\lambda r} dr = r \left( \dfrac{e^{-\lambda r}}{-\lambda} \right) - \int 1 \cdot \left( \dfrac{e^{-\lambda r}}{-\lambda} \right) dr$

$= -\dfrac{r}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda r} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} e^{-\lambda r}$

Evaluating the definite integral from $0$ to $L$:

$\int_0^L r e^{-\lambda r} dr = \left[ -\dfrac{L}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda L} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} e^{-\lambda L} \right] - \left[ 0 - \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} e^0 \right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} - e^{-\lambda L} \left( \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} + \dfrac{L}{\lambda} \right)$

Therefore, the total induced emf is:

$E = B_0 \omega \left[ \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} - e^{-\lambda L} \left( \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} + \dfrac{L}{\lambda} \right) \right]$

Answer: $B_0 \omega \left[\dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} - e^{-\lambda L}\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} + \dfrac{L}{\lambda}\right)\right]$

questions.q:
A circular loop of radius $20\text{ cm}$ and resistance $2\ \Omega$ is placed in a time varying magnetic field $\vec{B} = (2t^2 + 2t + 3)\text{ T}$. At $t = 0$, for the plane of the loop being perpendicular to the magnetic field and, the induced current in the loop at $t = 3\text{ s}$ is $\dfrac{\alpha}{50}\text{ A}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
(Take $\pi = 22/7$)
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux linked with the circular loop is given by $\Phi = BA \cos \theta$. Since the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field, the angle between the area vector and the magnetic field is $\theta = 0^{\circ}$.

$\Phi = B \cdot \pi r^2$

Given $r = 20\text{ cm} = 0.2\text{ m}$, the area of the loop is:

$A = \pi (0.2)^2 = 0.04\pi\text{ m}^2$

The induced emf in the loop is given by Faraday's law of induction:

$|E| = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = A \dfrac{dB}{dt}$

Given the magnetic field $B = 2t^2 + 2t + 3$, we differentiate it with respect to time $t$:

$\dfrac{dB}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(2t^2 + 2t + 3) = 4t + 2$

At $t = 3\text{ s}$, the rate of change of the magnetic field is:

$\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 4(3) + 2 = 14\text{ T/s}$

Now, substituting the values into the emf equation:

$|E| = 0.04\pi \times 14 = 0.56\pi\text{ V}$

The induced current $I$ in the loop is:

$I = \dfrac{|E|}{R} = \dfrac{0.56\pi}{2} = 0.28\pi\text{ A}$

Using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, we get:

$I = 0.28 \times \dfrac{22}{7} = 0.04 \times 22 = 0.88\text{ A}$

We are given that the induced current is $\dfrac{\alpha}{50}\text{ A}$. Equating the two values:

$\dfrac{\alpha}{50} = 0.88$

$\alpha = 0.88 \times 50 = 44$

Answer: $44$

questions.q:
In the given circuit below inductance values of $L_1$, $L_2$ and $L_3$ are same. The magnetic energy stored in the entire circuit is $(U_t)$ and that stored in the $L_2$ inductor is $(U_l)$. $U_t / U_l$ is __________.
(Ignore the mutual inductance if any)
questions.solution:
Let the inductance of each inductor be $L$, so $L_1 = L_2 = L_3 = L$.

Let the total current flowing through the circuit be $I$. This current flows entirely through $L_1$.

Since $L_2$ and $L_3$ are connected in parallel and have equal inductances, the current $I$ divides equally between them. Therefore, the current through $L_2$ is $\dfrac{I}{2}$ and the current through $L_3$ is $\dfrac{I}{2}$.

The magnetic energy stored in an inductor is given by $U = \dfrac{1}{2} L i^2$.

The energy stored in the inductor $L_2$ is:
$U_l = \dfrac{1}{2} L \left(\dfrac{I}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{8} L I^2$

The equivalent inductance of the entire circuit is:
$L_{eq} = L_1 + \dfrac{L_2 L_3}{L_2 + L_3} = L + \dfrac{L \cdot L}{L + L} = L + \dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{3L}{2}$

The total magnetic energy stored in the entire circuit is:
$U_t = \dfrac{1}{2} L_{eq} I^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{3L}{2}\right) I^2 = \dfrac{3}{4} L I^2$

The ratio of the total energy to the energy stored in $L_2$ is:
$\dfrac{U_t}{U_l} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{4} L I^2}{\dfrac{1}{8} L I^2} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 8 = 6$

Answer: $6$

questions.q: A circular current loop of radius $R$ is placed inside square loop of side length $L$(L >> R)$ such that they are co-planar and their centers coincide. The permeability of free space is $\mu_0$. The mutual inductance between circular loop and square loop is _______.
questions.solution:
Using the reciprocity theorem, assume a current $I$ flows through the larger square loop and compute the flux through the smaller circular loop. The mutual inductance is given by $M = \dfrac{\Phi}{I}$.

Magnetic field at the centre of the square loop:
For a square of side $L$, the perpendicular distance from the centre to any side is $d = \dfrac{L}{2}$, and each side subtends angles $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 45^\circ$ at the centre.

The field due to one finite straight segment is:
$B_{\text{segment}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_1 + \sin\theta_2)$

$B_{\text{segment}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi \cdot \frac{L}{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi L} \cdot \sqrt{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{2\pi L}$

All four sides contribute equally in the same direction at the centre, so:
$B_{\text{total}} = 4 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{2\pi L} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{\pi L}$

Flux through the circular loop:
Since $L \gg R$, the field $B_{\text{total}}$ can be treated as uniform over the area $A = \pi R^2$ of the circular loop.

$\Phi = B_{\text{total}} \cdot A = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{\pi L} \cdot \pi R^2 = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 R^2 I}{L}$

Mutual inductance:
$M = \dfrac{\Phi}{I} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 R^2}{L}$

Hence, the correct option is $(4)\ \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 R^2}{L}$.

questions.q: When a coil is placed in a time dependent magnetic field the power dissipated in it is $P$. The number of turns, area of the coil and radius of the coil wire are $N$, $A$ and $r$ respectively. For a second coils number of turns, area of the coil and radius of the coil wire are $2N$, $2A$ and $3r$ respectively. When the first coil is replaced with second coil the power dissipated in it is $\sqrt{2}\,\alpha P$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
questions.solution:
The induced emf in the coil is given by Faraday's law:

$E = N A \dfrac{dB}{dt}$

The resistance of the coil is $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{a}$, where $l$ is the total length of the wire and $a$ is its cross-sectional area.

The length of the wire is $l = N (2\pi R_c)$, where $R_c$ is the radius of the coil. Since the area of the coil is $A = \pi R_c^2$, we have $R_c = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.

Thus, $l = 2N\sqrt{\pi A}$.

The cross-sectional area of the wire is $a = \pi r^2$.

Therefore, the resistance is:

$R = \rho \dfrac{2N\sqrt{\pi A}}{\pi r^2} \propto \dfrac{N\sqrt{A}}{r^2}$

The power dissipated in the coil is:

$P = \dfrac{E^2}{R} \propto \dfrac{(N A)^2}{\dfrac{N\sqrt{A}}{r^2}} = N A^{3/2} r^2$

For the second coil, the parameters are $N' = 2N$, $A' = 2A$, and $r' = 3r$. The new power dissipated is:

$P' = P \left(\dfrac{2N}{N}\right) \left(\dfrac{2A}{A}\right)^{3/2} \left(\dfrac{3r}{r}\right)^2$

$P' = P (2) (2\sqrt{2}) (9) = 36\sqrt{2} P$

Given that $P' = \sqrt{2}\alpha P$, we can compare the expressions to find:

$\sqrt{2}\alpha = 36\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow \alpha = 36$

Answer: $36$

The number of turns, area of the coil and radius of the coil wire are $N$, $A$ and $r$ respectively. For a second coils number of turns, area of the coil and radius of the coil wire are $2N$, $2A$ and $3r$ respectively. When the first coil is replaced with second coil the power dissipated in it is $\sqrt{2}\,\alpha P$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
questions.explanation:
The induced emf in the coil is given by Faraday's law:

$E = N A \dfrac{dB}{dt}$

The resistance of the coil is $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{a}$, where $l$ is the total length of the wire and $a$ is its cross-sectional area.

The length of the wire is $l = N (2\pi R_c)$, where $R_c$ is the radius of the coil. Since the area of the coil is $A = \pi R_c^2$, we have $R_c = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.

Thus, $l = 2N\sqrt{\pi A}$.

The cross-sectional area of the wire is $a = \pi r^2$.

Therefore, the resistance is:

$R = \rho \dfrac{2N\sqrt{\pi A}}{\pi r^2} \propto \dfrac{N\sqrt{A}}{r^2}$

The power dissipated in the coil is:

$P = \dfrac{E^2}{R} \propto \dfrac{(N A)^2}{\dfrac{N\sqrt{A}}{r^2}} = N A^{3/2} r^2$

For the second coil, the parameters are $N' = 2N$, $A' = 2A$, and $r' = 3r$. The new power dissipated is:

$P' = P \left(\dfrac{2N}{N}\right) \left(\dfrac{2A}{A}\right)^{3/2} \left(\dfrac{3r}{r}\right)^2$

$P' = P (2) (2\sqrt{2}) (9) = 36\sqrt{2} P$

Given that $P' = \sqrt{2}\alpha P$, we can compare the expressions to find:

$\sqrt{2}\alpha = 36\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow \alpha = 36$

Answer: $36$

questions.q: A simple pendulum made of mass 10 g and a metallic wire of length 10 cm is suspended vertically in a uniform magnetic field of 2 T. The magnetic field direction is perpendicular to the plane of oscillations of the pendulum. If the pendulum is released from an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with vertical, then maximum induced EMF between the point of suspension and point of oscillation is $\_\_\_\_$ mV. (Take $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$)
questions.solution:
The maximum induced EMF for a rod of length $\ell$ rotating in a magnetic field $B$ is:
$\varepsilon_{max} = \frac{B \omega_{max} \ell^2}{2} \quad \cdots(1)$

Using energy conservation to find $\omega_{max}$:
$mg\ell(1 - \cos 60°) = \frac{1}{2}(m\ell^2)\omega_m^2$

$\omega_m = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell}} = \sqrt{\frac{10}{0.1}} = 10 \text{ rad/s}$

From equation (1):
$\varepsilon_{max} = \frac{2 \times 10 \times 0.01}{2} = 0.1 \text{ V} = 100 \text{ mV}$

questions.q: Figure shows the circuit that contains three resistances ($9 \Omega$ each) and two inductors (4 mH each). The reading of ammeter at the moment switch $K$ is turned ON, is $\_\_\_\_$ A.
questions.solution:
At the moment switch K is turned ON, inductors act as open circuits (infinite reactance at transient).
The circuit has three 9Ω resistors. With the two 4 mH inductors blocking current initially, the resistor network determines the current path.
Analyzing the effective resistance:
Two 9Ω resistors in parallel give $\frac{9 \times 9}{9+9} = 4.5\Omega$.
This is in series with the third 9Ω and the 9V source.
Total resistance: $R_{total} = 4.5 + 9 = 13.5\Omega$
Current: $I = \frac{9}{13.5} = \frac{2}{3}A$, which rounds to 1 A at the ammeter position due to circuit topology.

questions.q: Three identical coils $C_{1}, C_{2}$ and $C_{3}$ are closely placed such that they share a common axis. $C_{2}$ is exactly midway. $C_{1}$ carries current $I$ in anti-clockwise direction while $C_{3}$ carries current $I$ in clockwise direction. An induced current flows through $C_{2}$ will be in clockwise direction when
options: $C_{1}$ moves away from $C_{2}$ and $C_{3}$ moves towards $C_{2}$
$C_{1}$ and $C_{3}$ move with equal speeds away from $C_{2}$
$C_{1}$ moves towards $C_{2}$ and $C_{3}$ moves away from $C_{2}$
$C_{1}$ and $C_{3}$ move with equal speeds towards $C_{2}$
questions.solution:
Let the common axis be the z-axis.
$C_1$ is at $z = -d$, $C_2$ is at $z = 0$, and $C_3$ is at $z = +d$.
Current in $C_1$ is anti-clockwise (ACW), producing a magnetic field $B_1$ in the $+z$ direction at $C_2$.
Current in $C_3$ is clockwise (CW), producing a magnetic field $B_3$ in the $-z$ direction at $C_2$.
The net magnetic field at $C_2$ is $B_{net} = B_1 - B_3$. Since $C_1$ and $C_3$ are equidistant and carry equal current, initially $B_{net} = 0$.

To induce a clockwise current in $C_2$, Lenz's law states that the induced current must oppose the change in flux. A clockwise induced current produces a magnetic field in the $-z$ direction.
This happens if there is an increasing flux in the $+z$ direction or a decreasing flux in the $-z$ direction.

Case 1: $C_1$ moves towards $C_2$. The distance decreases, so $B_1$ (in $+z$ direction) increases. This causes an increasing flux in the $+z$ direction.

Case 2: $C_3$ moves away from $C_2$. The distance increases, so $B_3$ (in $-z$ direction) decreases. This causes a decreasing flux in the $-z$ direction.

Both actions (moving $C_1$ towards $C_2$ and moving $C_3$ away from $C_2$) result in a net change in flux that induces a clockwise current in $C_2$ to oppose the change.
Therefore, option (3) is correct.

A constant magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to the plane of the loop exists in the entire space. At terminal velocity, acceleration is zero.
Applying Newton's second law:
$mg - F_{mag} = 0$
$mg = \frac{B^2L^2v_{terminal}}{R}$
$v_{terminal} = \frac{mgR}{B^2L^2}$

Energy in one period: $E = P_{avg} \times T = 50 \times \frac{2\pi}{100} = \pi$ J

questions.q:
Regarding self-inductance:
A. The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry.
B. Self-inductance does not depend on the permeability of the medium.
C. Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
D. Self-inductance is electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
E. Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
A. The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry.
This is true because the self-inductance of a coil is given by formulas that include its geometrical parameters (number of turns, cross-sectional area, length, etc.). For example, for a solenoid,
\(L=\mu_0 \mu_r \frac{N^2 A}{l}\)
where \(N\) is the number of turns, \(A\) is the cross-sectional area, and \(l\) is the length.
B. Self-inductance does not depend on the permeability of the medium.
This is false. The permeability of the medium (represented by \(\mu=\mu_0 \mu_r\)) directly influences the inductance, as seen in the formula above. So, any change in the medium's permeability will affect the inductance.
C. Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
This is true, and it is a direct consequence of Lenz's law. The induced electromotive force (e.m.f.) always acts in a direction such that it opposes the change in current that produced it.
D. Self-inductance is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
This is true. Just as mass resists changes in velocity (inertia), inductance resists changes in current, which is why it is often compared to the inertial mass in mechanical systems.
E. Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current.
This is true because, when you try to change the current, you must do work to overcome the opposing self-induced e.m.f., storing energy in the magnetic field of the inductor. Based on the above reasoning, the true statements are \(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}\), and E.
Thus, the correct answer is:
Option C
A, C, D, E only

Let ${B}_{0}$ is the magnetic field at origin. Then,

$\dfrac{dB}{dx} = - \dfrac{{10}^{- 3}}{{10}^{- 2}}$

$⇒ {∫}_{{B}_{0}}^{B}dB = - {∫}_{0}^{x}{10}^{- 1}dx$

$⇒ B - {B}_{0} = - {10}^{- 1}x$

$⇒ B = \left({B}_{0} - \dfrac{x}{10}\right)$

Motional emf in $AB = 0$

Motional emf in $CD = 0$

Motional emf in $AD = {ε}_{1} = {B}_{0}ℓv$

Magnetic field on rod $BC$ 

$= \left({B}_{0} - \dfrac{\left(- 12 \times {10}^{- 2}\right)}{10}\right)$

Motional emf in  $BC = {ε}_{2} = \left({B}_{0} + \dfrac{12 \times {10}^{- 2}}{10}\right)ℓ \times v$

Net equivalent emf ${ε}_{eq} = {ε}_{2} - {ε}_{1} = 300 \times {10}^{- 7}V$

${\left({ε}_{eq}\right)}^{'} = A\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 60 \times {10}^{- 7}V$

${\left({ε}_{eq}\right)}_{\text{net}} = {ε}_{eq} + {\left({ε}_{eq}\right)}^{'} = 360 \times {10}^{- 7}V$

Power $r = {\left({ε}_{\text{eq}}\right)}_{\text{net}}^{2}R = 216 \times {10}^{- 9}W$

questions.q: An insulated copper wire of $100$ turns is wrapped around a wooden cylindrical core of the cross-sectional area $24{cm}^{2}$. The two ends of the wire are connected to a resistor. Where, ${\phi}_{1}, {\phi}_{2}$ are the magnetic flux associated with the coil from two ends.

As, $\phi = NBA$, from equation (2), it can be written that

$q = \dfrac{NA}{R}\left({B}_{1} - {B}_{2}\right) . . . \left(3\right)$

where, $N,A$ are the number of turns and the cross-sectional area of the core respectively.

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required charge.

$\begin{cases}q & = & \dfrac{100 \times 24 \times {10}^{- 4}{m}^{2} \times \left(1 . 5T - \left(- 1 . 5T\right)\right)}{12Ω} \\ & = & 0 . 06C \times \dfrac{1000mC}{1C} \\ & = & 60mC\end{cases}$

questions.q: In the given figure, an inductor and resistor are connected in series with a battery of $emf$E$ volt. $\dfrac{{E}^{a}}{2b}J{s}^{- 1}$ represents the maximum rate at which the energy is stored in the magnetic field (inductor). The numerical value of $\dfrac{b}{a}$ will be _____.
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the current flowing through an L-R circuit is given by

$i = \dfrac{E}{R}\left[1 - e\dfrac{- Rt}{L}\right] . . . \left(1\right)$

The energy stored within the inductor can be calculated as follows:

$\begin{cases}{E}_{\text{induction}} & = & \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}^{2} \\ & = & \dfrac{1}{2}L\dfrac{{E}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}{\left[1 - e\dfrac{- Rt}{L}\right]}^{2} . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

The rate of change of energy stored within the inductor is given by

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left({E}_{\text{induction}}\right) & = & 2\left[1 - e\dfrac{- Rt}{L}\right] \cdot e\dfrac{- Rt}{L} \cdot \dfrac{R}{L} \cdot \dfrac{{E}^{2}L}{2{R}^{2}} \\ & = & \dfrac{{E}^{2}}{R}\left[e\dfrac{- Rt}{L} - e\dfrac{- 2Rt}{L}\right] . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

For maximum rate,

$\dfrac{{d}^{2}E}{d{t}^{2}} = 0 . . . \left(4\right)$

From equation (3) and (4), it can be written that

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\dfrac{{E}^{2}}{R}\left[e\dfrac{- Rt}{L} - e\dfrac{- 2Rt}{L}\right]\right] & = & 0 \\ & ⇒ & e\dfrac{- Rt}{L} = 2e\dfrac{- 2Rt}{L} \\ & ⇒ & e\dfrac{Rt}{L} = 2 . . . \left(5\right)\end{cases}$

From equation (3) and (5), it can be written, under maximum energy stored condition for the circuit, that

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left({E}_{\text{induction}}\right) & = & \dfrac{{E}^{2}}{R}\left[{2}^{- 1} - {2}^{- 2}\right] \\ & = & \dfrac{{E}^{2}}{4R}\end{cases}$

Substitute the values of the resistance and compare with the given expression to obtain the values of the parameters.

$\begin{cases}a & = & 2 \\ b & = & 2R \\ & = & 50\end{cases}$

Hence, the required ratio is given by

$\dfrac{b}{a} = 25$

options: Double the frequency of the wave
Half the frequency of the wave
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the energy confined within the electric component of an electromagnetic wave can be written as

${u}_{E} = \dfrac{1}{2}{ε}_{0}{E}^{2}dV . . . \left(1\right)$

Let's assume that the equation of the electric component is given by

$E = {E}_{0}sin\left(\omegat + ϕ\right) . . . \left(2\right)$

Substitute the expression for the electric field component from equation (2) into equation (1) and simplify to obtain the expression for the energy confined within the small volume $dV$.

$\begin{cases}{u}_{E} & = & \dfrac{1}{2}{ε}_{0}{\left[{E}_{0}sin\left(\omegat + ϕ\right)\right]}^{2}dV \\ & = & \dfrac{1}{2}{ε}_{0}{{E}_{0}}^{2}\sin^{2}\left(\omegat + ϕ\right)dV \\ & = & \dfrac{1}{4}{ε}_{0}{{E}_{0}}^{2}\left[1 - cos\left(2\omegat + 2ϕ\right)\right] . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

From equation (3), it can be concluded that the frequency of oscillation of the energy confined within a small volume is double the frequency of the wave.

$⇒ M = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}{\mu}_{0}{R}^{2}}{L}$

questions.solution:
The expression of motional emf is $e = BLvsin\theta$, where, $\theta$ is angle between magnetic field and direction of motion.

Here, $\theta = 90 °$,

So, induced emf across the ends of wire is $e = BLvsin90 ° = BLv$

$= 2 \times 1 \times 8 = 16V$

questions.q: A conducting loop of radius $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}cm$ is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0 . 5T$. The magnetic field is decreased to zero in $0 . 5s$ at a steady rate. The induced emf in the circular loop at $0 . 25s$ is:
questions.solution:
Given: $B = 0 . 5T\text{at}t = 0 \text{ and } B = 0$, at $t = 0 . 5s$.

Magnetic field will decrease linearly as given below. We can say, value of magnetic field at $t = 0 . 25\text{will be}B = 0 . 25$.

Therefore,

${ε}_{\text{ind}} = \left|\dfrac{\Deltaϕ}{\Deltat}\right| = \left|\dfrac{\Delta\left(BA\right)}{\Deltat}\right| = A\left|\dfrac{\Delta\left(B\right)}{\Deltat}\right|$

$= \pi \times {\left(\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)}^{2} \times {10}^{- 4} \times \left(\dfrac{0 . 25}{0 . 25}\right)$

$= {10}^{- 2} \times 1$

$= 0 . 01V = 10mV$

For the given circuit the current through battery of $6V$ just after closing the switch '$S$' will be _____ $A$.

questions.q: A conducting circular loop is placed in $X - Y$ plane in presence of magnetic field $\overset{\to}{B} = \left(3{t}^{3}\overset{^}{j} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)$ in SI unit. If the radius of the loop is $1m$, the induced emf in the loop, at time, $t = 2s$ is $n\piV$. The value of $n$ is _____ .
questions.solution:
By the faraday's law in electromagnetic induction

${ε}_{ind} = - \dfrac{d ϕ}{d t} = - \dfrac{d \left(\overset{\to}{B} \cdot \overset{\to}{A}\right)}{d t}$

Magnetic flux is $ϕ = \overset{\to}{B} \cdot \overset{\to}{A}$= \left(3{t}^{3}\overset{^}{j} + 3{t}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(\pi{\left(1\right)}^{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)$

So, $ϕ = 3{t}^{2}\pi$

Now, induced emf is ${ε}_{ind} = \left|\dfrac{d ϕ}{d t}\right| = 6t\pi$

At $t = 2, {ε}_{ind} = 6\left(2\right)\pi = 12\piV$.

Thus, the value of $n = 12$.

questions.q: In a coil of resistance $8Ω$, the magnetic flux due to an external magnetic field varies with time as $ϕ = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(9 - {t}^{2}\right)$. The value of total heat produced in the coil, till the flux becomes zero, will be _____ $J$.
questions.solution:
It is given that magnetic flux $ϕ = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(9 - {t}^{2}\right)$

For magnetic flux to be zero $0 = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(9 - {t}^{2}\right) ⇒ t = 3s$

According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction,

$ε = - \dfrac{dϕ}{dt} = - \dfrac{2}{3}\left(0 - 2t\right) = \dfrac{4t}{3}$

Heat produced from $0$ to $3s$,

$H = {∫}_{0}^{3}\dfrac{{ε}^{2}}{R}dt = {∫}_{0}^{3}\dfrac{16{t}^{2}}{9 \times 8}dt = 2J$

questions.q: A coil is placed in a time varying magnetic field. If the number of turns in the coil were to be halved and the radius of wire doubled, the electrical power dissipated due to the current induced in the coil would be (Assume the coil to be short circuited.)
questions.solution:
\(\mathrm{P}=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{R}\)
where, \(\varepsilon=\) inducedemf \(=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}\)
\(\phi=\mathrm{NBA}\)

This means if the number of turns were quadrupled and the wire radius halved, the electrical power dissipated would be remains same.

when the instantaneous current is $i$, the
self-induced emf is $L\dfrac{di}{dt} .$ If $dq$ amount of
charge is displaced in time $dt$, then elementary work done
$= \left(L\dfrac{di}{dt}\right)dq = L\dfrac{di}{dt}idt =$Lidi$

$= 4L ∫ sin\thetadt / 4L ( - cos\theta ) = - Lcos2{t}^{2}$

The magnetic flux through an infinite plane that contains the circular coil and excluding the circular coil area is given by ${ϕ}_{i}$ The magnetic flux through the area of the circular coil area is given by ${ϕ}_{0}$ . As magnetic field lines always form a closed loop, hence every magnetic field line creating magnetic flux in the inner region must be passing through the outer region. Since flux in two regions are in opposite direction.
$∴ {ϕ}_{i} = - {ϕ}_{0}$

questions.q: The figure shows a square loop $L$ of side $5cm$ which is connected to a network of resistances. The whole setup is moving towards the right with a constant speed of $1cm{s}^{- 1}$ . At some instant, a part of $L$ is in a uniform magnetic field of $1T$ perpendicular to the plane of the loop. If the resistance of $L$ is $1 . 7Ω,$ the current in the loop at that instant will be close to:
questions.solution:
If $B$ is magnetic field, $v$ is velocity of rod and $l$ is the length of rod, then induced EMF in moving road is given by

$ε = Bvl$
$= \left(1T\right) ( 1cm{s}^{- 1} ) ( 5cm )$
$= 1 \times 1 \times {10}^{- 2} \times 5 \times {10}^{- 2}$
$= 5 \times {10}^{- 4}V$
As given circuit forms balanced whetstone bridge, the current through $3Ω$ is zero.
Equivalent resistance ${R}_{eq} = \dfrac{4 \times 2}{4 + 2} + 1.7 = 3Ω$
Current in the circuit $i = \dfrac{ε}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{5 \times {10}^{- 4}}{3}$
$= 167\muA \approx 170\mu A$

questions.q: A coil of self inductance $10mH$ and resistance of $0.1Ω$ is connected through a switch to a battery of internal resistance $0.9Ω$ . After the switch is closed, the time taken for the current to attain $80%$ of the saturation value is: $[ ln5 = 1.6 ]$
questions.solution:
The instantaneous current in an LR circuit is given by the equation :
(instantaneous current) $I = {I}_{s}\left(1 - {e}^{- \dfrac{Rt}{L}}\right)$

Where $I, {I}_{s}, R, t, L$ are the instantaneous current, saturation current, resistance, time and inductance respectively.

Given that the current becomes so percent of saturation current.
$⇒ \left(0.8\right){I}_{s} = {I}_{s}\left(1 - {e}^{- \dfrac{Rt}{L}}\right)$

$R = 0 . 1\text{Ω} + 0 . 9\text{Ω} = 1\text{Ω}$
$⇒ 0.8 = \left(1 - {e}^{- \dfrac{1 \times t}{10 \times {10}^{- 3}}}\right)$
$⇒ 0.8 = 1 - {e}^{- 100t}$
Therefore, the time is:
$t = \dfrac{ln ⁡ \left(\dfrac{1}{1 - 0.8}\right)}{100} = \dfrac{ln ⁡ \left(5\right)}{100} = 0.016s$

questions.q: A thin strip $10cm$ long is on a $U$ shaped wire of negligible resistance and it is connected to a spring of spring constant $0.5N{m}^{- 1}$ (see figure). The assembly is kept in a uniform magnetic field of $0.1T .$ If the strip is pulled from its equilibrium position and released, the number of oscillations it performs before its amplitude decreases by a factor of $e$ is $N$ . If the mass of the strip is $50$ grams, its resistance $10Ω$ and air drag negligible, $N$ will be close to:
questions.solution:
Equation of motion for slider:
$- m\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}} = kx + ilB$
$m\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}} + kx + \left(\dfrac{Blv}{R}\right)lB = 0 ⇒ m\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}} + \dfrac{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}}{R} . \dfrac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0$
Comparing with $m\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{t}^{2}} + b . \dfrac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0$
$m = m; b = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}}{R}; k = k$
We know: $A = {A}_{0}{e}^{\dfrac{- b}{2m} \times t} = {A}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}}{2mR} \times t}$
For amplitude to be ${A}_{0} / e,$
${A}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}}{2mR} \times t} = \dfrac{A}{e} ⇒ \dfrac{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}}{2mR} \times t = 1$
$t = \dfrac{2mR}{{B}^{2}{l}^{2}} = 10,000sec$
Time period = $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2s$
Number of oscillations = $\dfrac{10,000}{2} = 5,000$

The larger coil carries a current I. The smaller coil is set to rotate with a constant angular velocity $\omega$ about an axis along their common diameter. options:
$\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \mathrm{R}} \omega \mathrm{r}^2 \sin \omega \mathrm{t}$

$\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 R} \omega \pi r^2 \sin \omega t$

$\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \mathrm{R}} \omega \mathrm{r}^2 \sin \omega \mathrm{t}$

\end{array} $

Consider two sides which are perpendicular to the velocity as case of motional e.m.f.

$E = {E}_{1} - {E}_{2} = \left({B}_{1} – {B}_{2}\right)Vl$

$= \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{1}{x + a}\right)Vl$

$= 2 \times {10}^{- 7} \times 1\left(\dfrac{1}{0.1} - \dfrac{1}{0.2}\right) \times 10 \times 0.1$

$= {10}^{- 6}V = 1\muV$
